title: Black queer men in Camden | BLKOUT in Camden
metaDescription: For Black queer men in and around Camden — Camden Town, Kentish Town, Euston, Kilburn: what's here, what's beside us, what's worth the journey, and a community-owned door into BLKOUT.

landmark.alt: Pencil sketch of the Roundhouse's circular brick facade in Chalk Farm with the BLKOUT roundel set into a small moon above the roofline

hero.kicker: One community. Many doors. This one is Camden's.
hero.heading: BLKOUT in Camden
hero.standfirst: BLKOUT is a community-owned co-operative for Black queer men across the UK — and Camden's queer history runs deep: a Black-run molly house in the 1720s, a gay social circle around Regent's Park Road two centuries later, and — more recently — a good part of our own story. Black Men Who Brunch ran monthly from Old Diorama Arts Centre and Regent's Place from December 2019, and a picnic first nurtured by one of our own has grown into our biggest gathering of the year. Around 18,900 Black residents live in the borough now. This door is for the Black queer men among them.

quiz.heading: Know your Camden?
quiz.sub: Three questions. No prizes except the stories.

questions.q: Black Men Who Brunch — BLKOUT's own monthly gathering — started in Camden in which month?
questions.reveal: December 2019 — a taster event to "bring some realness to break up the Christmas schmaltz." It grew into a monthly fixture, reaching at least twelve editions by summer 2022, hosted at Old Diorama Arts Centre on Drummond Street and at Regent's Place, where British Land named BLKOUT an LGBT+ Community Partner.

questions.q: The BLKOUT Annual Picnic — now a Regent's Park fixture — began as whose event, before BLKOUT took on co-hosting it?
questions.reveal: Nzube Ufodike had nurtured the picnic for several years before asking BLKOUT to co-host in 2022. It's run every year since — 2026's edition, on the Camden side of Regent's Park near the zoo, raised money for LGBT+ Rights Ghana and closed with karaoke at Zodiac Bar.

questions.q: Ivor Cummings — already the anchor of our Croydon and Lambeth doors — belonged to a gay social circle of African and Caribbean intellectuals in 1930s and 40s London that contemporaries simply called...?
questions.reveal: "The group" — which also included the composer Reginald Foresythe and the singer John Payne, whose home at 17 Regent's Park Road was, in his contemporaries' words, "the place to be" for London's Black musical community. Paul Robeson stayed there; so did Marian Anderson and Ethel Waters.

scores.three: Camden knows its own history — because a good part of it is ours. Now help us write what's next.
scores.two: Close. Camden holds more of our own record than most boroughs ever will.
scores.low: All the more reason to walk through the door below — the history is the easy part to catch up on.

here.heading: Here in Camden
here.intro: What's organised in the borough for Black queer men and Black LGBTQ+ people, as we find it — and help us find more.
here.quietNote: Checked 3 September 2026 — we haven't found a space currently run by and for Black queer men in Camden, genuinely. Our own history here runs deep; a live, standing space doesn't yet. If one exists, or you want to start one, the panel below is where that begins.

besideUs.heading: Beside us in the borough
besideUs.intro: Neighbours doing good work in Camden. Use them — and tell them we sent you.

entries.name: Old Diorama Arts Centre
entries.note: Euston's community arts hub on Drummond Street, where Black Men Who Brunch ran for years — today it hosts 50+ local groups rent-free, including the London Trans Choir and Yas Queen! Chess Club.

entries.name: London Trans Choir
entries.note: London's first trans choir, non-auditioned and open to all, rehearsing at Old Diorama Arts Centre.

entries.name: Yas Queen! Chess Club
entries.note: Women-led, LGBTQ+-friendly chess club at Old Diorama Arts Centre, open to all.

entries.name: Camden People's Theatre
entries.note: A studio theatre built around artists facing systemic barriers — 66% of its commissioned artists are LGBTQIA+, 47% Global Majority. Staged GRILLS (2024), the show that brought the Camden Lesbian Centre and Black Lesbian Group's history back into the borough.

entries.name: ZODIAC Bar & Club
entries.note: Trans-founded by Jade Phoenix Hoskins in 2020, at 119 Hampstead Road since 2021 — over £300,000 raised for LGBTQ+ causes, and where BLKOUT's own Annual Picnic closes with karaoke. Reopened May 2026 after a fight to stay open; an active petition backs it.

entries.name: The Black Cap
entries.note: Camden Town's legendary drag cabaret pub, the "Palladium of drag" from the mid-1960s — Paul O'Grady debuted Lily Savage here in 1978. Closed 2015, reopened March 2026 after a decade-long campaign.

worthTheJourney.heading: Worth the journey
worthTheJourney.intro: Black queer men have never let a borough boundary decide where community happens. Where you're centred, not just welcome:

entries.name: Black Beetle Health
entries.note: The UK's only public health charity focused specifically on health inequalities for LGBTQ+ Black people and people of colour — resources, research and signposting, reachable from anywhere.

entries.name: Melanin Vybz — London LGBTQ+ Community Centre
entries.note: Bankside's community centre runs Melanin Vybz, a social space for Black and POC LGBTQ+ people — a short ride down the Northern line.

services.heading: Look after yourself
services.intro: Free, confidential, no GP needed, no judgement — and your business stays yours.

entries.name: Sexual Health London (SHL)
entries.note: Free, discreet home test kits and PrEP by post anywhere in London — order online, nothing to explain to anyone.

entries.name: Mortimer Market Centre
entries.note: Camden's own NHS sexual health and HIV clinic, on Mortimer Market off Tottenham Court Road — walk-in and booked appointments, PrEP, testing and treatment.

entries.name: 56 Dean Street
entries.note: Soho's LGBTQ+ specialist sexual health and HIV service — Europe's largest, and a short walk from Camden's southern edge.

entries.name: Find your nearest NHS clinic
entries.note: Every NHS sexual health service near you — testing, treatment, PrEP — searchable by postcode.

numbers.heading: The numbers nobody counts
numbers.body: The 2021 Census recorded 9.0% of Camden's population — around 18,900 people — as Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African, up from 8.2% in 2011. Camden doesn't rank among London's ten largest Black populations, so we don't have a dossier figure for it — but applying the same estimate we use elsewhere, that's roughly 400 to 630 Black queer men living in the borough right now. These are working estimates and we welcome correction. The point is the scale: we were never a niche. We were just never counted.
numbers.history:
Camden's Black queer history goes back further than most boroughs get to claim, and BLKOUT's own chapter is only the most recent of several.

In the 1720s, on or near Tottenham Court Road, a probably-free Black man named Julius Caesar Taylor ran a molly house — arrested and convicted in 1728 for "keeping a disorderly House" and "sodomitical Practices." It's one of the earliest documented instances of a Black man in London organising queer space for others, three hundred years before this door.

Two centuries later, a different kind of gathering formed around Regent's Park Road. John Payne, an American singer who'd settled in London after the First World War, bought a home at number 17 that became, in his contemporaries' words, "the place to be" for the Black musical and theatrical community — Paul Robeson stayed there, Marian Anderson and Ethel Waters passed through, and it was there that Lawrence Brown first met Robeson and began the musical partnership that lasted the rest of their lives. Payne was also part of what his friends simply called "the group": a gay social circle of African and Caribbean intellectuals in 1930s and 40s London that included the composer Reginald Foresythe and — already the anchor of our Croydon and Lambeth doors — Ivor Cummings, the civil servant who later welcomed the Windrush generation at Tilbury Docks. A few streets away in Primrose Hill, one genealogical record places bandleader Ken "Snakehips" Johnson on Gloucester Avenue in 1939 — a year before the Belgravia flat, shared with his partner Gerald Hamilton, where he was killed in the Blitz (now on our Westminster door); thinner sourcing, but a Camden thread of its own. And for thirty-eight years from 1929, the Grenadian-British cabaret star Leslie "Hutch" Hutchinson lived at 31 Steele's Road in Belsize Park — an English Heritage blue plaque marks the house today.

Organising took a different, collective shape in the 1980s. The Camden Lesbian Centre and Black Lesbian Group — with the Black Lesbian Group operating autonomously within it — opened its own building at 54-56 Phoenix Road on 31 October 1987, the UK's first and only dedicated lesbian centre. It ran until funding collapsed in the early 1990s, and its archive now lives four hundred miles away at Glasgow Women's Library. This is women's history, not this door's core focus, but it belongs in Camden's record — and in 2024 it came back into the borough itself, when Camden People's Theatre's GRILLS went looking for it and held a Black LGBTQ+ link-up for the group's former and current members after the show.

A century after Taylor, decades after Cummings and Payne, we added our own chapter. In December 2019 we launched Black Men Who Brunch — "a brand new monthly event that will be shaped for us, by us" — with founding partners Shade Free (the UK's Black-owned LGBT+ events brand) and Arboretum, a members' club. It grew fast: a February 2020 sequel, a run of themed editions through 2020 and 2021, and by February 2022 an eighth edition billed "Future History." Brunch found its home at Old Diorama Arts Centre on Drummond Street, and at Regent's Place — the Euston Road business estate where British Land named BLKOUT an LGBT+ Community Partner, with Triton Café hosting our monthly gatherings. By June 2022's twelfth edition, "Welcomes the Summer Kitchen," the series had, in our own words, "built and strengthened friendships and connections, put the world to rights, challenged loneliness and isolation, learned new skills from filmmaking to knitting."

Alongside it, a second Camden tradition took root outdoors. Nzube Ufodike had nurtured a summer picnic in Regent's Park for several years before asking BLKOUT to co-host in 2022 as the BLKOUTside Summer Picnic — new partners Slay Storiez, The Black Experience and the Black Boy Joy Collective joined that year, and a 'best dressed' theme became a running joke worth dressing up for. The tradition has run every year since. In 2026 it became the BLKOUT Annual Picnic: Sunday 16 August, on the Camden side of Regent's Park near the zoo, an unproduced day built to flex from a usual ~65 to hundreds — bring your crew, bring your sound — closing with karaoke at Zodiac Bar and a community collection for LGBT+ Rights Ghana.

We haven't found a space currently run by and for Black queer men in the borough — the panel below is where that gets built. But the ground has already been walked. If you were at a Brunch, or you've been coming to the picnic since before we were involved, the panel further down is where you tell us, and the page changes.

archive.intro: Our own story archive is being brought back online — the Brunch and picnic pieces referenced above are in our records but not yet republished with working links. When they are, they'll be listed here.

faq.q: Where can I meet other Black queer men in Camden?
faq.a: We don't have a standing one to point you to yet — genuinely, and we've checked. What we do have is history: BLKOUT's own Black Men Who Brunch ran here for years, and the BLKOUT Annual Picnic happens every August in Regent's Park. Start with the door on this page, and if a few Camden men want a table, we'll help hold it.

faq.q: Where can I get an STI test or PrEP in Camden?
faq.a: Sexual Health London posts free test kits and PrEP to any London address, no GP and no conversation required. Camden's own Mortimer Market Centre runs the borough's NHS sexual health clinic, and 56 Dean Street is a short walk away in Soho.

BLKOUT is one community-owned co-operative for Black queer men across the UK — with a door in every borough. We're registered in Croydon, but Camden is where a good part of our own history was made: Black Men Who Brunch and the picnic that became our Annual Picnic both started here.

faq.q: I'm not out. Can I still come?
faq.a: Yes. Come as you are — nobody at this door asks you to be anything first, and your business stays yours.

faq.q: Is the history on this page accurate?
faq.a: It's checked against our own records and the public record, and dated so you can see when we last looked — and where we couldn't find something current, including a standing Black-queer-men's space in Camden today, we've said so rather than guessed. If we've got something wrong, or you were part of a Brunch or a picnic we've missed, the panel at the bottom is where you tell us, and the page changes.

door.heading: Be met
door.tender: Come as you are. We answer.
door.intro: Leave your name and we'll keep you posted about Camden — what's on, what's starting, and how to be part of it. This goes to BLKOUT, a co-operative owned by its members. No engagement machinery, nothing sold onward — just a community that answers.

truer.heading: Make it truer
truer.intro: This is our own history more than most doors' — and it is still the people who were there who know it best. If you were at a Brunch, you're part of the picnic's older story, or a group's moved or folded — tell us. Corrections get credited, if you want the credit.

footer.line: BLKOUT is a member-owned Community Benefit Society for Black queer men in the UK. One platform, many doors — this one is Camden's.
